 Food pantry leaders weigh in on new proposed change to SNAP, gear up for Thanksgiving season
 ROCHESTER, N.Y. — Food pantries in the Rochester region are preparing for one of their busiest times of the year as Thanksgiving and the holiday season approach. 
 Pantry leaders say Thanksgiving is coming as many families are struggling with the effects of inflation and high gas prices. It also comes amid some changes to the SNAP food assistance program and a proposed change to who automatically qualifies. 
 RELATED: City launches plan to combat food insecurity, warns about rise in hunger since the pandemic 
 While food pantries are feeling the effects of higher food costs, support from partners like Foodlink and Wegmans has helped keep supplies steady. Foodlink, which stores and distributes millions of pounds of food to its partners across the 12-county region, is in the middle of its 33rd annual Check Out Hunger campaign to collect donations from Wegmans shoppers.
 Leaders at the People’s Pantry and Rochester Hope North Clinton Food Pantry say they’re able to meet the demand for fresh produce and meat for now, and hope to keep up with needs through the holiday season.
 “If there’s not a lot of free meats available or low-cost meats, I’m feeling it then. My monthly bill is feeling it then if I have to buy those kinds of things,” said Charyleah Cordone, executive director of People’s Pantry.
 “We are spending more money, but then we’re going to our donors and saying, hey, could you help us out a little bit? Everybody is so wonderful about that,” said Dawn Burdick, executive director of Rochester Hope North Clinton Food Pantry.
 RELATED: Foodlink is reaching hungry Rochester kids where they are this summer, but the funding won’t last 
 Changes to SNAP program
 There have been several federal policy changes to SNAP this year. Currently, able-bodied adults without dependents are required to work or volunteer to receive SNAP benefits, with some exceptions. In addition, the federal government is contributing less to SNAP funding, forcing county governments to spend more to keep the program running. Monroe County Executive Adam Bello said the county is responsible for finding an additional $4.3 million to keep SNAP funding the same. 
 There’s also another proposed change to SNAP. Last week, the U.S. Department of Agriculture proposed a rule that would stop people who get benefits under the Temporary Assistance for Needy Families program from automatically qualifying for SNAP benefits as well. The government is seeking public comment until next month, and if accepted, the rule would not take full effect for about two years.
 An estimated 5.5 million people nationwide have lost SNAP over the past year, according to the Associated Press. Executive directors at the People’s Pantry and Rochester Hope North Clinton Food Pantry say they’re against food assistance cuts during a time when thousands in the region rely on benefits to keep up with higher food costs. They said they are making sure they have volunteers and resources from Foodlink ready in case the changes take effect. 
 “Although some of them have talked a little bit about their benefits being cut a little bit, I am working more with the Rochester Works program for the able-bodied people that have to go out and either do a job or volunteer,” Cordone said.
 “It’s been proven that the money that you spend on SNAP helps the economy in general. Like if you’re purchasing things at the store, they have revenue, they employ people. And so it does have a trickle-down effect,” Burdick said.
 If the proposal goes through, the USDA estimates more than 6 million people could lose SNAP benefits by 2029. In Monroe County, about 100,000 people rely on SNAP, making up nearly 15% of the population.
 Pantries seeing an increase in demand
 Both food pantry directors said they already saw an increase in demand when new federal work requirements and SNAP food restriction waivers took effect in February. 
 Foodlink also says its demand is increasing. In August, Foodlink learned that its pantry partners have had the most visits on record. You can donate to Foodlink online here , or anytime you check out at a local Wegmans store. The Check Out Hunger Campaign runs through Nov. 28.
 In addition, many local food pantries are looking for volunteers. You can learn about volunteering at The People’s Pantry on Avenue D here and Rochester Hope North Clinton Food Pantry here .
 In-depth on food insecurity
 Over 12% of people in the 10-county region around Rochester faced food insecurity in 2024, according to the latest Map the Meal Gap report posted on Foodlink’s website . That amounts to over 155,000 people, including over 42,000 children.
 The City of Rochester is home to four zip codes with food-insecurity rates more than double the region’s average. The 14605 zip code had the highest at nearly 37%. Although the latest report shows a slight drop in food insecurity from 2023 to 2024, data collected by Foodlink showed a sharp rise in people seeking food assistance during the same time period.
